notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Judges 9:29–57, drawn from the sources I could access. (Fetch limits prevented me from opening every linked page fully, so where I rely on excerpts from search results rather than full page content, I note the limits.)

---

## v. 29 — Gaal’s Boast

**Traditional Reading**
Gaal, having gained the confidence of the Shechemites at a drunken feast in the house of Baal-berith, now openly voices what was in his heart all along: “If only this people were under my authority, I would remove Abimelech.” Gill explains that Gaal wished for rule over the city and command of its forces, and his challenge to Abimelech — “Muster your army and come out!” — was a blustering defiance meant to rally the Shechemites behind him (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/9.htm). Clarke calls Gaal’s speech “the very words and conduct of a sly, hypocritical demagogue” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-29.html). The *Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary* notes that Gaal had been waiting for someone else to propose his leadership; when no one did, he “ventures the proposal himself,” presenting his takeover as a favour to Shechem (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-9.html).

**Textual Note**
The words “he said to Abimelech” are widely understood as Gaal speaking *as if* Abimelech were present. The *Pulpit Commentary* adds that the people apparently embraced Gaal’s offer on the spot, and “thus emboldened, he sent a challenge to Abimelech to come out and fight him” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-9.html). Dummelow suggests a slight emendation: we should read “and I would say” rather than treating it as a direct address to Abimelech, who was in Arumah (v. 41) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/judges-9.html).

---

## vv. 30–31 — Zebul Informs Abimelech

**Traditional Reading**
Zebul, Abimelech’s “city manager” or governor in Shechem, heard Gaal’s words and “burned with anger.” The *Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary* notes that Zebul resented being dismissed as Abimelech’s mere “officer” (v. 28) and also feared being marked for destruction alongside his master (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-9.html). He sent messengers “covertly” (or “secretly,” as Enduring Word renders it) to Abimelech, reporting that Gaal and his brothers were stirring up the city (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

---

## vv. 32–33 — Zebul’s Plan

Zebul proposed a nighttime ambush: Abimelech and his troops should “lie in wait in the fields” and at sunrise rush the city. When Gaal and his men came out to fight, Abimelech could “do to them whatever you are able.” Enduring Word notes this was straightforward military advice for a surprise attack (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

---

## v. 34 — The Ambush in Four Companies

Abimelech followed Zebul’s advice, setting out by night and positioning his troops in “four companies.”

**A Literary Pattern**
Desiring God (John Piper) draws attention to a deliberate numerical spiral in Judges 9: Abimelech first divides his men into “four companies” (v. 34), then “three” (v. 43), then attacks with “two” (v. 44), and is finally slain by “one woman” (v. 53) — a downward pattern that highlights his decline (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/counting-with-god).

---

## vv. 35–36 — Gaal Sees the Troops; Zebul Deceives Him

At sunrise Gaal went out and stood at the city gate — just as Abimelech’s men rose from hiding. When Gaal said, “Look, people are coming down from the mountains!” Zebul mocked him: “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you.” Enduring Word says Zebul deliberately deceived Gaal to buy time for Abimelech’s forces to take position (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

---

## v. 37 — Gaal’s Second Report

Gaal persisted: he now saw people coming “from the center of the land” (or “the navel of the land,” possibly a reference to a high point in the region) and a company “by way of the Diviners’ Oak” (or “the Plain of Meonenim,” a terebinth associated with soothsaying). These topographical references are difficult to pin down precisely, but they underscore that Abimelech’s forces were closing in from multiple directions.

---

## vv. 38–40 — Zebul Taunts Gaal; Gaal Defeated

Zebul now dropped all pretence: “Where is your gloating now? You said, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ … Go out now and fight them!” Gaal had little choice. Constable notes that “Gaal probably was not prepared for a siege; so he had little choice but to leave the city walls behind and confront Abimelech out in the open” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-29.html). Gaal led the men of Shechem out, was routed, and fled. Many fell wounded “all the way to the entrance of the gate.”

---

## v. 41 — Aftermath of the First Battle

Abimelech “stayed in Arumah” (about five miles southeast of Shechem, per Constable), and Zebul “drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem.” The *Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary* observes: “From this moment, we hear no more of him. He disappears as one who goes down no more to rise. Zebul also is seen no more” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-9.html). Gaal vanishes from the biblical record.

---

## vv. 42–44 — The Second Attack: Three Companies

The next day, the people of Shechem — apparently confident the crisis was over — went out into the fields, likely to resume harvest work (Cundall, cited in Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/). Abimelech was informed. He divided his men into three companies and ambushed them: one company seized the city gate, and the other two massacred the people in the fields.

---

## v. 45 — Shechem Destroyed and Sown with Salt

Abimelech fought against the city all day, captured it, killed its inhabitants, demolished it, and “sowed it with salt.” This is the only biblical instance of this symbolic act.

**Traditional Interpretations**
- Keil & Delitzsch (quoted by Constable): “Strewing the ruined city with salt … was a symbolical act, signifying that the city was to be turned for ever into a barren salt desert” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-29.html).
- Peake’s Commentary: “To sow a city with salt was to declare symbolically that it was henceforth to be as fruitless and desolate as a salt desert,” while noting that “in the case of Shechem, nature itself made that impossible” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/judges-9.html).
- The *Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary* offers another angle: salt was a symbol of covenant. The Shechemites had made a covenant with Abimelech in the house of Baal-berith; sowing the city with salt signified that “for the breach of that covenant … they were devoted to destruction” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-9.html).
- The *Pulpit Commentary* notes that salt destroys vegetation and was used by gardeners for that purpose, citing Pliny: “*Omnis locus in quo reperitur sal sterilis est*” — every place in which salt is found is barren (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-9.html).

Constable notes Shechem was not rebuilt until Jeroboam I, nearly two centuries later (1 Kings 12:25) (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-29.html).

---

## vv. 46–49 — The Massacre at the Tower of Shechem

Hearing of Abimelech’s destruction, the leaders of the tower of Shechem (often identified with Beth-millo, a citadel) fled into the inner chamber of the temple of El-berith (also called Baal-berith). Abimelech led his men up Mount Zalmon, cut a branch with his axe, put it on his shoulder, and told his men: “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” Each man followed suit. They piled the branches against the inner chamber and set it on fire, killing “about a thousand men and women.”

**Traditional Readings**
- Enduring Word calls this a graphic fulfilment of Jotham’s curse (Judges 9:19–20): fire came from the bramble and devoured them. It also cites Trapp: “This was as if a man should run into a stack of straw or barrel of gunpowder, to secure himself from a raging fire” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).
- The *Pulpit Commentary* thinks many who perished “had taken sanctuary there, not occupied it for the purposes of defence” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-9.html).
- The *Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary* adds that Abimelech “understood some basic principles of leadership” — he led by personal example, albeit for evil purposes (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-9.html).

**Reformed View**
Ligonier notes that Abimelech “burning much of the city and its defensive tower” was God’s instrument of judgment on Shechem for its complicity in the murder of Gideon’s sons. The lesson: “Tolerating sin in the camp will bring destruction” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/danger-from-within).

---

## vv. 50–52 — Abimelech Attacks Thebez

Not satisfied with destroying Shechem, Abimelech marched to Thebez (modern Tubas, about 13 miles north of Shechem), encamped against it, and captured it. The inhabitants fled into a strong tower inside the city. Abimelech approached the tower door “to set it on fire” — apparently confident after his success at the tower of Shechem (Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

---

## v. 53 — A Woman Crushes Abimelech’s Skull

A woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, “crushing his skull.” This is the pivotal moment of divine retribution.

**Details about the Millstone**
- Gill and other older commentators identify this as the upper stone of a hand-mill, the kind women used for daily grinding (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/9.htm).
- Constable cites studies suggesting such hand-stones averaged 10–14 inches long and weighed about five pounds (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-53.html).
- Wesley notes the justice of God: Abimelech slew his brothers “upon a stone” and now dies by a stone (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/judges-9.html).

**The “Poetic Justice” Theme**
Multiple traditions highlight this:
- Ellicott: “The murderer of his brothers ‘on one stone’ is slain by a stone flung on his head, and the treacherous idolaters are treacherously burnt in the temple of their idol” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-9.html).
- Trapp (cited in Enduring Word): “Upon one stone he had slain his seventy brethren, and now a stone slayeth him: his head had stolen the crown of Israel, and now his head is smitten” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).
- Peake’s: “In the field of destiny men reap as they have sown” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/judges-9.html).

---

## vv. 54–55 — Abimelech’s Death and the Army’s Dispersal

Mortally wounded, Abimelech called hastily to his armour-bearer: “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” The young man thrust him through, and he died.

**Traditional Readings**
- Matthew Henry offers an extended reflection on Abimelech’s pride: “The man was dying, but his pride was alive and strong … As God punished his cruelty by the manner of his death, so he punished his pride by the instrument of it.” Henry adds that by ordering his own killing, Abimelech “became a self-murderer” and actually perpetuated the very disgrace he sought to avoid — since Joab later refers to this incident (2 Samuel 11:21) (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/9-53.html).
- Enduring Word notes the irony: “Yet long after his death, the credit continued to be given to the woman (cf. 2 Samuel 11:21)” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).
- Ellicott observes: “The death of a leader was generally sufficient to break up an ancient army” — and indeed, when the men of Israel saw Abimelech dead, “they all went home” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-9.html).

---

## vv. 56–57 — God’s Retribution and Jotham’s Curse Fulfilled

The narrator closes with a theological summation: “In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.”

**Traditional Readings**
- Gill: These verses contain “the remarks made upon this history by the writer of it, who, in all probability, was the Prophet Samuel.” He notes the shedding of such blood “required blood to be shed again” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/9.htm).
- The *Pulpit Commentary* highlights that the sacred writer “marks especially the conduct of Abimelech as undutiful to his father,” connecting it to the fifth commandment (Exodus 21:17; Matthew 15:4). Each evidence of God’s righteous judgment is “a presage of the judgment to come” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-9.html).
- Ellicott: “These impressive verses give the explanation of the whole narrative … God punishes both individual and national crimes, and … men’s pleasant vices are made the instruments to scourge them” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-9.html).

**Reformed Emphasis**
Ligonier stresses God’s sovereignty in retribution: “Thus God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech … And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads.” The application is that “tolerating sin in the camp will bring destruction” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/danger-from-within).

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic)**
David Guzik writes: “We can be certain that God will repay wickedness, either in this life or the life to come. Often God finds a way to do it both in this life and the life to come” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On this passage, major Protestant traditions largely agree on the meaning — the narrative is a clear case of divine retribution. Differences are subtle and mostly in emphasis:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises God’s sovereign orchestration of judgment. God “sent an evil spirit” (v. 23) to create discord — this is divine agency in judgment, not merely permission. The application focuses on the danger of tolerating sin within the covenant community (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/danger-from-within).

- **Baptist (Gill, Desiring God):** Gill focuses on verse-by-verse exposition of the Hebrew text with historical-grammatical precision. Desiring God (Piper) treats the chapter as an example of how God works redemptively even through “messed-up families” — Abimelech is presented as part of a broader biblical pattern of sinful dysfunction through which God’s grace ultimately shines (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/gods-mercy-in-messed-up-families).

- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke, Wesley):** Clarke calls Gaal a “sly, hypocritical demagogue,” showing a concern with moral character. Wesley’s notes highlight the “justice of God … suiting the punishment to his sin” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/judges-9.html).

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Guzik provides lively application, emphasising that God’s judgments are certain in this life and the next, and that “rejecting God’s warnings … carries a real and terrible price” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-9/).

- **Lutheran and Anglican:** No distinct readings emerged from the searched sources. The LCMS and 1517.org sites did not appear in results.

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Peake’s Commentary)**
Peake’s notes that verses 42–49 “seem to contain a second, independent account of the attack on Shechem,” suggesting the narrative may have been compiled from two sources. It also notes that “D” (the Deuteronomist) “makes no contribution” here — apparently the Deuteronomistic editor “did not regard Abimelech as worthy to rank among the Judges, and therefore he omitted this section, which was restored to its place by R” (the Redactor). Peake’s also describes Abimelech’s death scene as “strikingly like that of Saul” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/judges-9.html).
